rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine names vary in scope in correspondence with their effects: knowledge branches into hearing, sight, imagination, and understanding, while broader provision and mercy encompass further qualities.
rows.anchor: موهبة العلم التي عندنا تنشعب منها شعب السمع والبصر والخيال والتعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names form a hierarchy from specific names to the all-encompassing greatest name; effects and blessings widen with a name's generality, and all effects ultimately submit to it.
rows.anchor: حتى تنتهي إلى اسم الله الأكبر الذي يسع وحده جميع حقائق الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A popular belief treats the greatest name as an unknown verbal formula that guarantees a response and can subject everything to human will.
rows.anchor: شاع بين الناس أنه اسم لفظي من أسماء الله سبحانه إذا دعي به استجيب

rows.speaker: أصحاب العزائم والدعوات
rows.claim: Practitioners of invocations claim the name has a naturally indicative utterance, with letters varying by need and methods for extracting and composing them.
rows.anchor: وفي مزعمة أصحاب العزائم والدعوات أن له لفظا يدل عليه بطبعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports suggest a verbal composition: the basmala is especially close to the greatest name, its letters occur in cited passages, and Asif used its letters to bring the Queen of Sheba's throne instantly.
rows.anchor: وما ورد أن آصف بن برخيا وزير سليمان دعا بما عنده من حروف اسم الله الأعظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says the greatest name has seventy-three letters, of which God gave the prophets seventy-two and reserved one in the unseen.
rows.anchor: أن الاسم الأعظم على ثلاث وسبعين حرفا قسم الله بين أنبيائه اثنين وسبعين منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Real causal influence depends on the strength of existents and affinity between cause and effect; a sound or mental concept cannot overpower existence because it is itself dependent on human will.
rows.anchor: فإن التأثير الحقيقي يدور مدار وجود الأشياء في قوته وضعفه، والمسانخة بين المؤثر والمتأثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine names, including the greatest name, mediate effects in the cosmos through their realities; God acts through the fitting attribute, not through a word, mental concept, or independent entity.
rows.anchor: لكنها انما تؤثر بحقائقها لا بالألفاظ الدالة في لغة كذا عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to answer a caller (2:186) requires a true request directed to God; one who turns from every other cause reaches the reality of the name suited to the need, whose effect follows its scope.
rows.anchor: فمن انقطع عن كل سبب واتصل بربه لحاجة من حوائجه فقد اتصل بحقيقة الاسم المناسب لحاجته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports and prayers about the greatest name should be understood as connection to the name's reality; teaching a servant a name opens this way of turning to God, while words and meanings only preserve realities.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا يجب أن يحمل ما ورد من الروايات والأدعية في هذا الباب دون الاسم اللفظي أو مفهومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name may be exclusive to God; al-Ilāh is exclusive as a proper name, whereas al-Raḥmān has a shared meaning as one of the beautiful names.
rows.anchor: أن الاسم الخاص ربما يطلق على ما لا يسمى به غير الله سبحانه كما قيل به في الاسمين الله، والرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah is a proper name exclusive to God rather than a name in the technical sense under discussion; al-Raḥmān has a shared meaning, and the legal inquiry lies outside this exegetical discussion.
rows.anchor: أما لفظ الجلالة فهو علم له تعالى خاص به ليس اسما بالمعنى الذي نبحث عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scripture does not set a fixed number of beautiful names: 20:8, 7:180, and 59:24 indicate that every name whose meaning is most beautiful belongs to God.
rows.anchor: لا دليل في الآيات الكريمة على تعين عدد للأسماء الحسنى تتعين به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author enumerates the divine names found in the Qur'an, grouping them alphabetically by their Arabic initials.
rows.anchor: والذي ورد منها في لفظ الكتاب الإلهي مائة وبضعة 127 وعشرون اسما هي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names belong to God essentially and originally; others possess their meanings only derivatively by God's gift, and that gift does not remove them from God's ownership.
rows.anchor: فهو المالك لها حقيقة، وليس لغيره إلا ما ملكه الله من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Comparative forms such as al-Aʿlā and al-Akram, and genitive forms such as best of judges and providers, imply that divine and human referents share a basic meaning.
rows.anchor: فإن صيغة التفضيل تدل بظاهرها على اشتراك المفضل والمفضل عليه في أصل المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no exegetical proof that divine names are restricted to transmitted forms; the opposing argument assumes both a covenantal reading of the article and that illicit naming means exceeding transmitted names, and both assumptions are questionable.
rows.anchor: وكلا الأمرين مورد نظر لما مر بيانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The well-known report that God has ninety-nine names and that whoever enumerates them enters Paradise does not prove that names are restricted to that number.
rows.anchor: إن لله تسعة وتسعين اسما مائة إلا واحدا من أحصاها دخل الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetically the names are not restricted to transmitted forms, while legal caution favors using only transmitted names for formal naming; ordinary predication is less restricted.
rows.anchor: والاحتياط في الدين يقتضي الاقتصار في التسمية بما ورد من طريق السمع

rows.speaker: علي عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report transmitted in al-Tawḥīd through al-Riḍā and his forefathers says that invoking God by ninety-nine names brings a response and enumerating them leads to Paradise; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains enumeration as faith in all their meanings.
rows.anchor: عن الرضا عن آبائه عن علي عليه السلام إن لله عز وجل تسعة وتسعين اسما

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet's saying that God has ninety-nine names and whoever enumerates them enters Paradise, for God is singular and loves the singular.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abū Nuʿaym and Ibn Mardawayh transmit from Abū Hurayra a variant saying that God has one hundred names less one, and that calling on them brings a response; al-Dāraquṭnī gives a divine-speech variant of the ninety-nine-name report.
rows.anchor: أقول رواها عن أبي نعيم وابن مردويه عنه، ولفظه قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn ʿUmar report the Prophet saying that God has ninety-nine names and whoever enumerates them enters Paradise; one wording adds that they are in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: أخرج أبو نعيم وابن مردويه عن ابن عباس وابن عمر قالا قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that all ninety-nine enumerated names occur in the Qur'an conflicts with later lists containing names not found there verbatim, unless it means that their meanings occur in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: والرواية تعارض ما سيأتي من روايات الإحصاء حيث إن جميعها مشتملة على أسماء ليست في القرآن بلفظها

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: A report in al-Tawḥīd, transmitted through al-Ṣādiq's forebears from ʿAlī, repeats the Prophet's statement that God has ninety-nine names and whoever enumerates them enters Paradise.
rows.anchor: عن الصادق عن آبائه عن علي عليه السلام قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage continues the transmitted enumeration of divine names, including Allah, al-Ilāh, al-Wāḥid, al-Aḥad, al-Ṣamad, and al-Awwal.
rows.anchor: وهي الله، الإله، الواحد، الأحد، الصمد، الأول، الآخر، السميع، البصير، القدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah is included in enumerations so that the other names can be predicated of Him; it is otherwise outside the count.
rows.anchor: وذكر لفظ الجلالة في هذه الروايات المشتملة على الإحصاء لإجراء الأسماء عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The quoted report repeats that God has ninety-nine names and whoever enumerates them enters Paradise.
rows.anchor: إن لله تسعة وتسعين اسما من أحصاها دخل الجنة

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله جعفر بن محمد الصادق عليه السلام
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq says the ninety-nine names are found in the Qur'an and assigns them to individual suras, listing five in al-Fātiḥa and thirty-three in al-Baqara among others.
rows.anchor: عن الأسماء التسعة والتسعين التي من أحصاها دخل الجنة فقال هي في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura-by-sura report is confused: it counts Allah among the names, repeats names such as al-Kabīr, totals 110 despite initially saying ninety-nine, and disputes whether some names occur in the cited suras.
rows.anchor: فإن فيه إدخال لفظ الجلالة في الأسماء التسعة والتسعين وليس منها، وقد كرر بعض الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The available enumeration reports do not restrict God's beautiful names to their lists: they disagree, include names absent verbatim from the Qur'an, and omit Qur'anic names; at most, ninety-nine names carry the special promise of response and Paradise.
rows.anchor: لا تدل على انحصار الأسماء الحسنى فيما تحصيها مع ما فيها من الاختلاف في الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports and transmitted prayers of the Prophet and the Imams show that God's names exceed ninety-nine and include many names absent from the Qur'anic enumeration lists.
rows.anchor: أن هناك روايات أخرى تدل على كون أسمائه تعالى أكثر من تسعة وتسعين

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report in al-Kāfī describes a nonphysical, unspoken divine name with four simultaneous parts: three names were revealed to meet creation's needs and one hidden, stored name was concealed; each revealed name has four pillars, each producing thirty names or acts.
rows.anchor: إن الله تبارك وتعالى خلق اسما بالحروف غير متصوت، وباللفظ غير منطق

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: The report says the names ultimately reach 360, related to the three revealed names that serve as pillars and conceal the hidden name, and cites the command to call God by Allah or al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: فهذه الأسماء وما كان من الأسماء الحسنى حتى تتم ثلاثمائة وستين اسما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The described name cannot be a word or a mental concept; it is the referent matched by a word, namely the transcendent essence or something inseparable from it.
rows.anchor: فليس المراد بالاسم إلا المصداق المطابق للفظ لو كان هناك لفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creating a name means the divine essence manifests in a way that yields a name, fitting the hierarchy in which names mediate for one another and end at a name whose determination is itself undetermined.
rows.anchor: أن المراد به ظهور الذات المتعالية ظهورا ينشأ به اسم من الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah, Tabāraka, and Taʿālā point respectively to the essence gathering all perfection, the affirmation of perfections and bestowal of blessings, and the removal of deficiencies and needs.
rows.anchor: وهي ثلاث جهة استجماع الذات لكل كمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report's names attributed as acts to the pillars express the author's principle that one name gives rise to another.
rows.anchor: وهو إشارة إلى ما قدمناه من انتشاء إسم من اسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report's count of 360 names explicitly shows that divine names are not limited to ninety-nine.
rows.anchor: صريح في عدم انحصار الأسماء الإلهية في تسعة وتسعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concealed name is still a manifestation of the divine essence, yet its hiddenness means its manifestation and determination are absent; even the claim that God exceeds every description remains a human description that cannot encompass Him.
rows.anchor: فظهوره عين عدم ظهوره وتعينه عين عدم تعينه
